newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: U.S. seeks cooperation from Saudis on Khobar bomb.
newsitem.headline: U.S. seeks cooperation from Saudis on Khobar bomb.

text.p: U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen on Sunday pressed Saudi Arabian leaders to provide more information to U.S. authorities in the investigation of a terrorist bombing in Saudi Arabia last June that killed 19 U.S. troops.

Cohen told reporters following a meeting in Jeddah with Crown Prince Abdullah and Defence Minister Prince Sultan that Abdullah replied that "full cooperation would be given" in the incomplete Saudi bombing investigation.
The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) has complained about a lack of Saudi help on the unsolved truck bomb blast at Khobar Towers military housing complex in Dhahran last June 25.
No blame has been assigned for the attack and no determination made on whether an outside country sponsored it.

"I don't have the specifics of what the FBI needs. But I just indicated that they felt that they needed more information. And he (Abdullah) indicated that...full cooperation would be given," Cohen told reporters on his plane en route to Kuwait from Jeddah on the second leg of a Gulf visit.
"He responded that it was in all of our interests -- their interests as well as our interests, to give as full cooperation as possible, that anything that needed to be done he felt would be done."
Cohen said he had "reiterated what President (Bill) Clinton had said, that we expect full cooperation and we expect we will receive it."
Prince Abdullah is considered the most powerful Saudi official after King Fahd.

Cohen, who met the king on Saturday, said the Sunday meeting was cordial and Abdullah and Sultan expressed strong support for U.S.-Saudi ties and backed Washington's policy of "dual containment" of Iran and Iraq in the Gulf.
Cohen was having dinner in Kuwait City on Sunday night with Kuwait's Defence Minister Sheikh Salem Sabah al-Salem al-Sabah and was to meet Kuwait's Emir Sheikh Jaber al-Ahmad al-Sabah on Monday.
Earlier on Sunday, Cohen and the commander of U.S. military forces in the Gulf visited a sweltering Prince Sultan air base in the Saudi desert and met some 4,000 U.S. troops stationed there.

Army General Binford Peay, head of the U.S. Central Command with responsibility for U.S. forces in the Gulf, told reporters that Iraq's air force had recently increased training exercises including limited night flights.
But Peay also said that Iraq air forces, decimated in the 1991 Gulf War, posed no threat to U.S. and allied air power despite increased training.
"In the past three months we have seen an increase in their flying posture. They have even begun a very little night training," he said.

"But compared against the advantage of our people, they don't fit in the same league," Peay told reporters, adding that dozens of U.S., British and French attack jets sometimes flew as many as 200 daily missions over southern Iraq to keep watch over President Saddam Hussein's military.

The defence secretary, wearing a dark suit and tie in 47 degrees Celsius (117 Fahrenheit) heat, told some of the U.S. air force troops that threats from Iran and Iraq would not drive the U.S. military from the Gulf.
"We are determined to protect our interests and theirs," Cohen said of the powerful U.S military presence in Saudi Arabia and other moderate Gulf states since the war with Iraq.
"We are going to have a U.S. presence as long as there remains a threat to the Gulf area," he added.
The U.S. air force along with French and British forces moved attack jets and crews to the remote base 90 miles (145 km) south of Riyadh for safety after the bombing.

Allied jets based in Saudi Arabia and Kuwait fly daily over southern Iraq, monitoring compliance with an allied no-fly zone order to Saddam not to attack Shi'ites in the region or build up his forces for any new strike against Kuwait, a move that started the Gulf War.
Peay said Iraq's exercises did not take place in extreme southern Iraq or in a similar no-fly zone in northern Iraq.
